thread.title_full: Sharpshooters to begin reducing deer population in Worthington - NewsBreak

author: Gracie Collins
title: Sharpshooters to begin reducing deer population in Worthington - NewsBreak
text:
By Gracie Collins ,
5 hours ago
WORTHINGTON, Ohio ( WCMH ) — Starting Thursday, sharpshooters will be able to begin operations in Worthington’s residential neighborhoods to reduce the deer population. However, one resident is temporarily protected from it happening on their property.
“Our issue to me is not a deer issue. It’s a safety issue,” said Kevin Callinan, a Worthington resident.
He filed a lawsuit against the city after receiving a letter that his property may be used for culling deer. Callinan cited safety concerns and not wanting his two children to have to see the deer be killed.
“I understand it could be a necessity, but I don’t see why it has to infringe on my family’s ability to use their property,” he said.
A Franklin County judge granted a temporary order blocking the city from shooting deer within 1,000 feet of his home. A spokesperson with Worthington told NBC4 that they are working to prepare a legal response and next steps.
“Safety is our top priority,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “This program is based on proven best practices used successfully in communities across Ohio and the country. We are working directly with federal and state wildlife professionals who have extensive experience managing similar programs with strong safety records. Every aspect of the program is guided by community input and expert safety standards. The City has spent several years studying this issue and gathering extensive community input. We had thousands of residents respond through two community surveys and 73% supported the use of firearms by trained experts as a deer management tool. This feedback helped inform Council’s decision-making and formed the basis of our program.”
According to community surveys in Worthington, 73% approved of the operation.
“They are obviously very overpopulated. It’s becoming a hazard for cars, for residents and especially for the deer. There’s just not room for them here,” said Worthington resident Melanie Koss.
The sharpshooters are from the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service-Wildlife Services. They will primarily work on weekdays after dark but some residents still have their reservations.
“I don’t like the idea of, you know, these high-powered rifles within our city limits, because all it takes is one thing to go wrong,” Margarita Crow said.
The program is set to last until Feb. 28, but may get extended into March. Learn more about the operation here.
